source.title: Homophily modulates double descent generalization in graph convolution networks
source.authors: Cheng-Zhi Shi; Li-Ming Pan; Hong Hu; Ivan Dokmanić

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures test risk while varying training-label ratio and relative model complexity, testing double-descent behavior with graph neural networks and a different analytical and experimental setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own test-risk curves for label-ratio sweeps and relative-model-complexity sweeps. It also reports risk changes with graph noise and regularization. Exact curve ordinates that are only shown in figures are recorded as figure only. Numerical values used to set graph-noise levels or select self-loop strengths are not treated as double-descent results.
record.test_reason: The study measures test risk directly in a new setting, transductive node classification with graph networks. It sweeps the training-label ratio τ on real and synthetic graphs, and sweeps relative complexity α=F/N analytically for a simple (linear-in-weights) GCN on CSBM. Results bear on V3 (more labels hurt), V4 (a non-deep model class whose risk falls past interpolation) and V6 (noise and regularization dependence). There is no model-size sweep of deep networks, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that transductive double descent, a regime where more labels hurt, is common in GNNs as the label ratio varies. Its shape and presence are modulated by graph homophily, graph and feature noise, and implicit or explicit regularization. A replica-method analysis of simple GCNs on CSBM predicts these curves precisely and also shows double descent versus relative model complexity. A further conclusion is that negative self-loops improve performance on heterophilic graphs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses transductive node classification with GCNs, graph datasets, CSBM analysis, label-ratio sweeps, and a relative-complexity sweep; it does not reproduce the original deep-network training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with graph homophily or heterophily, graph and feature noise, architecture, and regularization strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative self-loops (A+cI with c<0) improve GCN and FSGNN accuracy on heterophilic graphs, e.g. FSGNN on Chameleon rises from 78.27% to 78.96% (Table 1, Figs. 6–7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal self-loop sign and strength in GCNs depend on graph homophily.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: Several results are available only as plotted curves without extractable numerical ordinates. Many experimental data points are averaged over 10 trials; the reported variability is standard deviation. The main theoretical analysis is for simple GCNs on a stylized model, and the graph-matrix universality result is presented as a conjecture.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying result was omitted from the paper's explicitly described risk trends. Exact point-by-point values in Figs. 1–7 and 12 are not extractable from the supplied text and are recorded as figure only.

untested.parts: No sweep of deep-network size. The multi-layer GNNs are swept only over label ratio; the α sweep is for a one-layer linear GCN.
No effective-complexity measure. The ridgeless theory places the peak at γτ=1 (labels = features), the plain interpolation threshold, and does not test a unified measure across axes.

Label noise specifically (only graph and feature noise are varied); triple or multiple descent; optimally tuned regularization (only 'large r' is tested, and the optimal-regularization claim is cited).
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure.

missing.what: Texas results: one-layer GCN accuracy decreases near-monotonically with τ and there is no interpolation peak (γ=0.11); 'too many labels seems detrimental'.
Ridgeless CSBM theory and experiment: test risk explodes at γτ=1 (λ=μ=1, γ=5, r=0), matching the closed form in Eq. 18.
Fig. 5A (large r gives monotone risk) and Fig. 5C (mild double descent at α near 1).
Columns 3–4 of Fig. 1 (dropout; cross-entropy loss) on Cora, Chameleon and Texas: dropout and nonlinearity alleviate the effect.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 labels were moved to V4: the α sweep is a theoretical curve for a one-layer, activation-free ridge GCN, not a deep network. The paper is by the same broad research line but is not an original source. Most real-data results are qualitative (figure only); several rows pool multiple models under one statement.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests relative model complexity in simple GCNs and reports qualitative results for some real-data GNN settings, but not the broader claim for deep networks generally.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The study varies the fraction of observed node labels in transductive learning; it does not test arbitrary training-sample-size settings outside that context.

The study does not test capacity growth past interpolation across model classes. Its results on several architectures primarily vary training-label ratio; its model-complexity sweep is for a simple GCN.
The paper relates the interpolation condition to its parameters, but does not test whether one measure of effective complexity predicts peak location across all three axes.
The study examines graph and feature noise and regularization, not label noise specifically; it does not test triple or multiple descent.
No test of whether re-counting complexity by an effective parameter measure turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
